## Part A — Creating Vectors: c(), seq(), rep()
```{r}
scores <- c(88, 92, 79, 95, 84)
scores
subjects <- c("Math", "Science", "English", "History", "PE")
subjects

## Use seq()
odds <- seq(1, 19, by = 2)
odds

evenly_spaced <- seq(0, 1, length.out = 5)
evenly_spaced

## use rep()

a <- rep("A", 4)
a
b <- rep(c("A", "B"), each = 2)
b
c <- rep(c("A", "B"), times = 2)
c

## Question #1\
  age <- c(15, 28, 32, 36, 27, 18, 52, 39, 42, 29, 35, 31, 27, 22, 37, 34, 19, 20, 57, 49, 50, 37, 46, 25, 17, 12, 42, 53, 41, 51, 35, 24, 33, 8)
  age
  
  #a. How many data points?
  length(age)
  
  #b. Find the reciprocal of age?
  1 / age
  
  #c. Assign also new_age <- c(age, 0, age). What happens to new_age? 
  new_age <- c(age,0,age)
  new_age
  #It combines age, the number 0, and age again into one vector. Since age has 34 data points, new_age has 69 data points.
  
  #d.Find the minimum and the maximum value of age.
  min(age)
  max(age)
  
  ## Question #2
  # each = 2 repeats every element twice before moving to the next one. times = 2 repeats the whole vector twice.
  
  ##Question #3
  #by = 2 increases the numbers by 2 each time, producing odd numbers from 1 to 19. length.out = 5 creates exactly 5 evenly spaced numbers between 1 and 20. I would use by when I need a fixed interval and length.out when I need a specific number of values.
  
  
  ##Question #4
  #a.
  vec_num <- seq(20, 60)
  vec_num
  
  #b.
  mean(vec_num)
  
  #c.
  sum(vec_num)
  
  #d.
  length(vec_num)
  
```

## Part B — Subsetting (Accessing) Vectors

```{r}
grades <- c(88, 92, 79, 95, 84)
names(grades) <- c("Math", "Science", "English", "History", "PE")
grades[3]
grades[c(1, 4)]
grades[c("Science", "PE")]

grades[-c(1, 4)]
grades[grades >= 85]

#Question 5: Negative indexing is useful when I want to remove specific data, such as excluding the first and fourth grades from a list. Logical indexing is better when I want to select data that meets a condition, such as finding all students who scored 85 or higher.

#Question 6: 
grades[10]
#R returns NA because the tenth element does not exist in the vector, which only contains five elements. It does not throw an error because R allows out-of-range indexing and represents the missing value with NA.

Filter(function(i) {
  all(i %% c(3, 5, 7) != 0)
}, seq(100))
```

## Part C — Vector Operations and append()
```{r}
x <- c(1, 2, 3, 4)
y <- c(10, 20, 30, 40)
x + y
x * 2


z <- c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6)
short <- c(1, 0)
z + short


fruits <- c("apple", "banana", "cherry")
append(fruits, "date")
append(fruits, "kiwi", after = 1)

#Question 8: R's recycling rule repeats the shorter vector until it matches the length of the longer vector. In this example, short contains 1 and 0, so R repeats them as 1, 0, 1, 0, 1, 0 before adding them to z.

#Question 9
z + c(1, 0, 1)
z + c(1, 0, 1, 1)
#To explain, R recycles the shorter vector to perform the addition. It recycles silently when the longer vector's length is an exact multiple of the shorter vector's length. If it is not an exact multiple, R still performs the operation but gives a warning.
```

## Part D — Lists: Creating and Subsetting

```{r}
student <- list(
  name = "Maria Santos",
  age = 20,
  grades = c(88, 92, 79),
  is_enrolled = TRUE
)
student["grades"]
class(student["grades"])
student[["grades"]]
class(student[["grades"]])

student$name
student$grades[2]

#Question 10: Single brackets [ ] return a list containing the selected element, so student["grades"] has the class "list". Double brackets [[ ]] extract the actual contents of the selected element, so student[["grades"]] returns the numeric vector of grades.

#Question 11: A vector usually stores elements of one basic data type, while a list can contain different types of data, such as text, numbers, logical values, and other vectors. R uses [ ] to select one or more list elements and [[ ]] to extract one element's contents directly. This makes it easier to organize and access different kinds of information.
```

## Part E — Critical Thinking Challenge
```{r}
inventory <- list(
  item = c("Notebook", "Pen", "Eraser"),
  price = c(25.50, 10.00, 5.00),
  in_stock = c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE)
)

inventory$item[inventory$in_stock]

inventory$item <- append(inventory$item, "Ruler")

inventory$price <- append(inventory$price, 15.00)

inventory$in_stock <- append(inventory$in_stock, TRUE)

inventory

#Question 12: First, inventory$item accesses the vector containing the product names. Next, inventory$in_stock accesses the vector of TRUE and FALSE values. The logical condition selects the positions where the stock status is TRUE. R then uses those same positions to select the product names, returning only Notebook and Pen because Eraser is out of stock.

#Question 13: Keeping related information in separate vectors can cause problems if items are added, removed, or reordered in only one vector. The product names, prices, and stock statuses might no longer match correctly. A list groups related vectors under one object, making the data easier to organize. For a growing inventory, I would prefer a data frame because each product can be stored as a row, with its name, price, and stock status in separate columns. This makes filtering, sorting, and updating the inventory easier and reduces the risk of mismatched data.
```

## Conclusion
```{r}
#Vectors in R store elements of the same basic data type, while lists can store different types of data, such as numbers, text, and logical values. Vectors are useful for performing calculations and working with a collection of similar data. Lists are better when organizing related information with different data types, such as a student's name, age, and grades. I would choose a vector for simple data and a list when I need to group different kinds of information into one object.
```
